en: The Scripture on the Funeral Rites after the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa. One fascicle. Translated by an anonymous monk;
now appended to the Western Jin Record.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the World-Honored One was traveling through the kingdom of Pāṭaliputra. Ānanda, by means of human concentration...
Then, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"After the World-Honored One has passed away, what are the rites for the enshrinement and interment of your venerable body?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Furthermore, you should worry only for yourself and not worry about the Buddha.
After my parinirvāṇa, there will be brahmins and householders who will perform the funeral rites with full ceremony. Ānanda said:
“What are the rites for this?
The World-Honored One replied:
“They are like the ceremonial protocols for the funeral procession of a Cakravartin Emperor.”
He asked again,
"I wish to hear the rules of conduct.
The World-Honored One said:
"When the Holy Emperor passed away, his body was wrapped in a thousand pieces of karpāsa cotton cloth; fragrant oils were poured over it so that they permeated down through the body.
His body was then encased in a fragrant firewood pyre, with the layers above, below, and on all four sides made uniform.
Fire was set to cremate him, the bones were collected, washed with fragrant liquid, and placed within a golden urn."
There were stone basins—three feet in length and breadth, and one foot in thickness—one placed at each of the four sides and one at the top and bottom—with a golden jar set in the center.
Adorning the sacred site with suspended silk banners and providing all necessary offerings, they built a stupa of earth and made offerings of flowers and incense.
The Buddha was to pass beyond it.

Why was this so? Because for countless kalpas, I have practiced the four immeasurables with great compassion and cultivated the six perfections (pāramitās). Weaving through the ten directions, I have rescued and saved all living beings; my merit and virtue are magnificent and radiant, such that I have become this Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, the Supreme One, the Peerless One.
Each person who offers a handful of earth as an offering to a stupa gains immeasurable merit.
In the defiled and turbid final age, people will face lives of hardship and turmoil, and their wealth will be divided among five families.
For this reason, I have retained the śarīra relics along with the bowl to alleviate the calamities and upheavals of the world and to bring peace and protection to all sentient beings.

By establishing ancestral temples and images so that the people may behold them, and by having the śramaṇas guide and transform others through the sutras according to what has not yet been heard, I shall cause those who live to forever depart from the cruelty of the prison and those who die to escape the sins of the three miserable realms, ensuring they will surely attain rebirth in heaven.
"If it is for a Buddhist temple, it shall exceed that.
Ānanda asked, "What then should be done with the bowl?"
The Buddha said:
"My bowl was offered by the Four Great Heavenly Kings; they joined four together to make one.
This vessel from which the Buddha eats—beings must take care not to eat from it."

After his parinirvāṇa, the various kingdoms will contend with one another; the people’s minds will become perverse and wild, they will hold life cheap and lust dear, and they will turn their backs on filial piety while honoring demons.
At that time, the bowl shall manifest transformations, displaying light of five colors, flying and ascending and descending, thereby enlightening and transforming the people's hearts.

When the common people beheld this, they commemorated the Buddha’s virtues; they abandoned ignorance for enlightenment and followed the correct teachings. They all established temples and monasteries to honor and manifest the Buddha’s virtues.

When he subsequently travels eastward, in all the lands he passes through, calamities and epidemics shall be extinguished; rulers and ministers shall enjoy peace and well-being; grain and silk shall be abundant; and all shall rejoice without affliction. Ultimately, they shall distance themselves from the three miserable realms and all attain rebirth in the heavens.
The King of the Far East is benevolent and enlightened; the bowl shall fly thither.
After the king’s demise, his successor will be licentious and dissolute, abandoning the truth for the heterodox;
the people’s minds will likewise follow suit, and they will show no reverent decorum upon beholding the bowl.
When the devas and nāgas saw this, they met with both grief and joy; they welcomed the bowl back to the ocean to offer it in worship.

The King, having lost his honored bowl, felt a mixture of sorrow and indignation in his breast; he issued a proclamation throughout all the kingdoms, offering a thousand pieces of gold in exchange for the bowl.
He recruited people year after year, ordering them to track down the leader and the followers.
The people, greedy for the heavy rewards, searched everywhere but found nothing.
At that time, there was a lowly man named Shi who falsely assumed the guise of a bhikṣu; he was gluttonous for food and drink, yet maintained a wife and raised children.
At that time, Druma’s son went to the palace gate and said,
"I know the location of the bowl.
When the king heard this, he was greatly delighted and invited the śramaṇa inside, saying:
"Where is the bowl? He replied,
"I have already brought the gold."
The king bestowed a thousand *kārṣāpaṇas* upon him.
The Master said,
"Only a śramaṇa should steal this."
He immediately issued a decree to investigate and interrogate the śramaṇas; their treatment was so cruel and fierce that among the ministers and subjects, there were none who did not resent the king.
The king asked: "Whose śramaṇas are you?"
He replied, "My teacher serves the Buddha.
The king said:
"What precepts does the Buddha have?
The teacher replied,
"There are two hundred and fifty precepts."
The King asked: "What is the first precept? He replied:
"First, one should revere loving-kindness (*maitrī*).
One should bestow benevolence and universal grace upon all living beings, regarding the lives and bodies of all beings in the world as one's own life and body;
providing compassionate relief and pity, exercising empathy to bring peace to others, rejoicing in the Way and transforming them, and protecting others as one protects oneself."
"The moisture reaches even the grasses and trees, leaving nothing empty,
stunted, or severed. The King said, "Excellent!"
The Buddha’s benevolent transformation embraces heaven and envelops the earth; what living being does not rely upon it?
"Second, one should follow purity.
Do not accumulate impure treasures; honor the state, for usurpation exists neither through existence nor non-existence."
"Even among things as insignificant as grass and weeds,
I do not take them unless they are given. The King said, "Excellent!"
"This may be called being pure and clean.
"Third, one should follow integrity.
Let there be no lust in the mind and no lewdness in speech; as for false sounds and depraved sights, do not look at or listen to them even once."
"Behold that woman as a mother, a sister, a younger sister, or a daughter;
rather than committing sexual misconduct, it would be better to burn one's own body. The king said:
"Excellent! To grasp the true and pure landscape, one must take the Buddha as the head.
"Fourth, one should be cautious with speech."

They abstain from double-tongued speech, harsh abuse, false speech, and frivolous chatter; they do not praise one person to their face while disparaging them behind their back; they do not testify falsely against the innocent; nor do they employ sorcery, demonic arts, malevolent incantations, or curses.
"It would be better to swallow charcoal than to let out a poisonous sound.
The King said, "Excellent is the Buddha's transformation!"
"Apprehensive and trembling, one must be cautious with speech even to this extent.
"Fifth, one must abstain from wine.

Now, wine causes rulers to be unkind, ministers to be disloyal, parents to be unrighteous, sons to be unfilial, and women to be extravagant and licentious. Its faults number thirty-six; there is no ruin of states or destruction of families that does not stem from this."
"It would be better to drink poison and die than to live in the disorder of alcohol.
The King said, "Excellent!"
The Buddha’s enlightened transformation causes one to internalize virtue and embrace the Way, extinguishing all evils and promoting all forms of goodness;
it takes purity as the body and detachment as the aspiration.
The Sūtras transform people to cultivate benevolence, yet you teach me to kill;
the Precepts speak of maintaining purity and freedom from greed, yet you steal gold;
the Precepts speak of abstaining from lust, yet you keep a wife.
"One should observe the precepts with utmost sincerity; yet you have falsely slandered the śramaṇa, claiming he stole my bowl and thereby making me guilty of an innocent crime.
One should abstain from intoxicants, yet you have come here drunk."
"Are there not other śramaṇas outside [this community] who possess these five virtues and practice as exalted conductors? He replied,
"Their wickedness and impurity are even greater than mine."
The King asked the officials,
"What is the occupation of these śramaṇas? They replied:
"To beg for alms without moderation is far more defiling than that teacher of yours.
The King said, "The Buddha’s precepts number two hundred and fifty; your virtue exceeds even the decorum of the benevolent!"
Pure as the Great Primordial!
Upright and aligned with empty space!
Faithful as the four seasons!
How brilliant it is that you can leap across the sun and moon!
Is it because you have obtained such a class of people who usurp the dharma-robes, steal the alms-bowls, falsely claim to be śramaṇas, and bring disorder to the true and authentic?
You do not observe even a single precept, yet you speak of the two hundred and fifty.
He issued an edict to the relevant officials, saying:
"The temple of the Buddha is a sanctuary of purity, revered by the worthy and the sages; it is not a den for birds and beasts.
Expel those who are defiled and turbid, so that they do not remain within the Buddha’s temple."

"The gentlemen of the land desire to promote the temple for the sake of benefit, yet they are unable to find a worthy person to dwell therein and proclaim the divine transformations of the Buddha; thus, they stop with tears in their eyes.
Since then, the Great Way has declined, and divine transformations have waned day by day."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Although I shall pass into parinirvāṇa, I leave behind this bowl and my relics. If there are worthy ones who serve them with a reverent mind, they shall all ultimately ascend to heaven."

Ānanda said: "If at the end of a thousand years, this almsbowl manifests such divine virtue and transformations, how much more so must be the numinous transformations of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Way, the Most Perfect Enlightenment?"
When the Buddha preached this sutra, the devas, nāgas, spirits, kings, ministers, and the fourfold assembly were all moved to tears; they prostrated themselves and departed.
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, [this] scripture was used for the enshrinement and funeral rites.
